Gujarat state energy authorities and power discoms are facing an unprecedented grid emergency as electricity demand reached an all-time record peak of 29,822 MW on Friday, surprisingly eclipsing the state's highest summer consumption recorded in June.
The sharp surge—triggered by an intense late October heatwave and severe El Niño-induced rainfall deficits—has forced farmers to run agricultural pumps non-stop for groundwater extraction. With rural agricultural feeders taking priority to save standing crops, state utilities have implemented mandatory power staggering and unannounced supply cuts across major manufacturing hubs, hitting industrial operations hard.
October Heat Surpasses Summer Peak Demand
Electricity consumption across Gujarat has defied seasonal trends by climbing well past peak summer levels. In June, maximum peak demand hovered between 26,834 MW and 28,833 MW. However, persistent dry winds, high afternoon temperatures, and a prolonged monsoon dry spell have pushed current daily consumption to a record 586 million units (MU), up from 529 MU during the previous high.
With surface water sources depleting rapidly due to deficit monsoon rainfall, thousands of high-horsepower tubewells across rural districts are drawing heavy electric loads around the clock. The sudden reliance on underground water pumping has shifted the main weight of the state's power load from urban air-conditioning to rural agricultural feeders.
Power Cuts and Staggering Hit Key Industrial Belts
To prevent grid failure while supplying continuous electricity to rural agricultural networks, power distribution companies have initiated power staggering and rotational supply cuts in industrial zones. Manufacturing clusters in key belts like Sanand and Dahej are facing unexpected load shedding and operational slowdowns.
Small and medium enterprises warn that forced staggering schedules are disrupting automated assembly lines, damaging machinery, and throwing delivery commitments off schedule. Local industry bodies have raised serious concerns over the sudden rationing of industrial power.
Emergency Supply Coal and Grid Coordination
State energy planners report that the current demand curve shows no sign of flattening as October heat continues across northern and central districts. To manage the ongoing deficit, Gujarat has urged the Ministry of Power to release additional allocations from unallocated central generating reserves.
Simultaneously, state thermal plants are seeking priority coal rake shipments from the Coal Ministry to maintain adequate stock levels during this extended peak period. With long-term forecasts pointing to sustained weather volatility, power utilities are forced to balance heavy rural agricultural irrigation demands against the continuous supply needs of industrial estates.
